title: The New York Indian Film Festival Just Turned 25. Its Lineup Reads Like a Thesis on Where Indian Cinema Is Going.
excerpt: From Nawazuddin Siddiqui's meta-film about fame to a Shyam Benegal 4K restoration to an AI ethics drama in Hindi — NYIFF's silver jubilee edition arrived with something for every corner of the diaspora.
body:
For a quarter of a century, the New York Indian Film Festival has operated as a quiet counterweight to Bollywood's commercial machinery. While multiplexes in Edison and Jackson Heights fill up for the latest masala entertainers, NYIFF screens the films that festival programmers believe will define Indian cinema's future — films that rarely get North American theatrical runs, films in languages that mainstream distributors ignore, films made by directors who cannot afford marketing budgets.

The 25th edition, which ran from May 28 through June 1 at the Village East by Angelika in Manhattan, was arguably the festival's most ambitious yet. And for NRIs who pay attention to Indian cinema beyond the weekend box office numbers, the lineup read like a roadmap.

## The Films That Mattered

The centerpiece screening was Kennedy, Anurag Kashyap's noir thriller that premiered in Cannes' Midnight Section. Starring Rahul Bhat — who earned widespread acclaim for his role in the streaming hit Black Warrant — alongside Sunny Leone, the film tackles corruption and personal demons in Kashyap's characteristically unflinching style.

But it was the closing night film, Little Thomas, that captured NYIFF's ethos most precisely. A coming-of-age dramedy set in 1990s Goa, it marks the directorial debut of Kaushal Oza and stars Rasika Dugal and Gulshan Devaiah, both of whom attended the festival alongside the crew.

The narrative lineup spanned seven languages and a striking range of concerns. Humans in the Loop, directed by Aranya Sahay, explores the ethics of artificial intelligence in a near-future India — a premise that lands differently when your audience includes the engineers building the systems the film critiques. I'm Not An Actor stars Nawazuddin Siddiqui in what is being described as a searing meta-critique of fame and identity — a subject Siddiqui, a two-time NYIFF Best Actor winner, is uniquely positioned to explore. Angammal, adapted from a Perumal Murugan short story, examines women's agency in rural Tamil Nadu. Village Rockstars 2 marks Rima Das's return to the Assamese children's music narrative that earned her international acclaim and a National Award.

## Honoring the Masters

NYIFF dedicated a special segment to Shyam Benegal, the titan of Indian parallel cinema who passed away in 2024. The festival screened a 4K restoration of Manthan (1976), his landmark film about India's White Revolution, restored by the Film Heritage Foundation. The film originally premiered at Cannes Classics in 2024, and its NYIFF screening represented one of the few opportunities for diaspora audiences to see it on a proper cinema screen.

Also on the slate was An Arrested Moment, a Metropolitan Museum of Art short documentary directed by Dev Benegal, exploring Oscar-winner James Ivory's lifelong fascination with Indian art and culture — a pairing that felt particularly resonant in a Manhattan venue.

## The Diaspora Lens

"What began as a grassroots platform is now a global stage for Indian independent cinema," Festival Director Aseem Chhabra said. "This year's lineup is one of our most powerful and wide-ranging to date. We are especially proud to welcome back stalwarts like Goutam Ghose, Rima Das, Suman Ghosh and Nikhil Mahajan, while also shining a spotlight on extraordinary new talent."

Suman Gollamudi, Executive Director of the Indo-American Arts Council which presents NYIFF, added: "At 25, we are not just celebrating the past — we are investing in what's next."

The documentary programming underscored that point. A Fly on the Wall, by Shonali Bose and Nilesh Maniyar, documents physician-assisted suicide in Switzerland. Marching in the Dark examines the widows of farmer suicides in Maharashtra. Turtle Walker follows a conservationist protecting India's sea turtles. These are not crowd-pleasing subjects, but they reflect the kind of cinema that NYIFF exists to champion — stories that commercial distributors overlook because the audience is small, even as that audience is deeply engaged.

## Why It Matters for the Community

For the Indian diaspora in the tristate area, NYIFF serves a function that streaming platforms cannot replicate. It creates a physical space where independent Indian cinema meets its most committed American audience. The closing night after-party at Chatti, chef Regi Mathew's buzzy new Manhattan restaurant known for contemporary Kerala cuisine, reinforced the point: this is not just a festival but a community gathering, one that has persisted through 25 years of shifting tastes, pandemic disruptions, and the relentless pressure of commercial cinema's dominance.

Tickets, schedules, and program details are available at nyiff.us.
author: Diaspora Desk
